overview: Hijaz is a western Arabian region, not one state lasting from 600 to 1945. This atlas uses “hejaz” for 600 to 800 and “hejaz-1920” for 1920 to 1945, with a 1,120-year gap. A shared place-history card is useful because both polygons include Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, Rabigh, al-Ula, and al-Bahah. Their governments were radically different. In the early window, Medina became the center of Muhammad's community and the first caliphs; authority then shifted through civil wars to Damascus-based Umayyads and Baghdad-based Abbasids. In the modern window, Hussein's Hashemite Kingdom of the Hejaz, proclaimed in 1916, survived only until Saudi conquest in 1925. Ibn Saud ruled a dual kingdom, and in 1932 it became Saudi Arabia. The atlas nevertheless keeps a separate Hejaz layer through 1938 and removes it only at 1945. Its modern polygon even contains Najran and Sana'a, so it is an atlas envelope, not a surveyed frontier. Pilgrimage, ports, roads, families, schools, water systems, and written Arabic connect the regional story; they do not make its successive regimes one continuous country.

periods.title: 600 to 622: western Arabia before the Medinan polity
periods.summary: Mecca, Yathrib, later Medina, and other oasis and port communities belonged to a connected but politically varied western Arabian region. The atlas paints a single Hejaz polygon from 600, but neither that shape nor the regional name establishes one government. Muhammad's migration to Yathrib in 622 begins a new political chapter.

periods.title: 622 to 632: Muhammad's community at Medina
periods.summary: After the Hijra, agreements at Medina organized obligations among several believing, allied, and Jewish groups. Muhammad's community grew into the leading regional power and Mecca came under its authority in 630. The evidence describes negotiated membership and conflict, not a modern nation-state filling the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 632 to 656: Medina and the first caliphs
periods.summary: Medina remained the seat of the first caliphs while conquest expanded far beyond the Hijaz. Sacred authority, legal memory, and political decisions accumulated there. Expansion did not turn the regional Hejaz layer into a separate empire; it sat inside a rapidly changing caliphate whose reach the local polygon cannot represent.

periods.title: 656 to 692: capitals move and civil war reaches Mecca
periods.summary: Ali moved his capital to Kufa in 656, and the Umayyad dynasty ruled from Damascus after 661. Ibn al-Zubayr later claimed the caliphate from Mecca until Umayyad forces defeated him in 692. The holy cities remained central, but political authority was contested and no continuous “Hejaz state” governed this interval.

periods.title: 692 to 750: Umayyad authority and pilgrimage politics
periods.summary: Abd al-Malik restored Umayyad control after the second civil war. Mecca and Medina retained religious prestige, scholarly networks, and political importance while the imperial center remained Damascus. Pilgrimage leadership and patronage mattered greatly, yet the atlas's regional color should not be mistaken for a sovereign Hijazi kingdom.

periods.title: 750 to 800: Abbasid rule and road investment
periods.summary: The Abbasids replaced the Umayyads in 750 and governed from Iraq, founding Baghdad in 762. Investment in pilgrimage routes, wells, pools, and stations linked distant travelers to Mecca and Medina. At 800 the atlas removes “hejaz” and paints a broad Abbasid layer, an editorial relabeling rather than the region disappearing.

periods.title: 800 to 1517: a region under changing outside and local powers
periods.summary: After 800, Abbasid authority weakened and western Arabia passed through several imperial, dynastic, and local arrangements. Sharifian rulers in Mecca became durable regional actors while claiming or receiving recognition from larger powers. This long bridge explains continuity of place and pilgrimage without inventing uninterrupted sovereignty for the atlas label.

periods.title: 1517 to 1916: Ottoman framework and sharifian government
periods.summary: Ottoman sovereignty and local sharifian authority overlapped in the Hijaz for centuries. Pilgrimage administration, Red Sea trade, and eventually the railway connected the region to a wider empire. The arrangement ended amid the First World War and Arab Revolt, not at the atlas's later 1920 starting seam.

periods.title: 1916 to 1925: the Hashemite Kingdom of the Hejaz
periods.summary: Hussein proclaimed the Kingdom of the Hejaz during the Arab Revolt. Wartime siege, uncertain recognition, financial strain, and competing claims shaped the new monarchy. Saudi forces took Taif, Mecca, Medina, and Jeddah in 1924 and 1925; Ali's surrender ended the Hashemite kingdom in December 1925.

periods.title: 1925 to 1945: Saudi conquest, dual kingdom, and regional continuity
periods.summary: Ibn Saud became King of the Hejaz in 1926 and ruled the Kingdom of the Hejaz and Nejd from 1927. A 1932 decree renamed the combined state the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The Hijaz continued as a region and administrative sphere; 1945 marks only the atlas layer's removal, not a new conquest.

items.text: The index contains exactly two missing records named Hejaz: “hejaz” from 600 to 800 and “hejaz-1920” from 1920 to 1945. Their imported summaries are byte-identical, but the 1,120-year gap and radically different authorities forbid presenting them as one continuous state. Both ids should open one explicitly regional card.

The early feature appears in the 600 and 700 snapshots with one identical 29-position polygon. It contains tested points at Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, Rabigh, Khaybar, al-Ula, and al-Bahah. These are reproducible properties of imported geometry, not proof of a surveyed seventh-century border.

The modern feature appears in 1920, 1930, and 1938 with one identical 65-position polygon. It shares eight tested regional places with the early shape but also contains Tabuk, Najran, and Sana'a. Including Sana'a makes the warning especially plain: this is an oversized atlas envelope, not the Kingdom of Hejaz's legal frontier.

At 800, the atlas removes the regional Hejaz feature and assigns its tested core to the broad Abbasid layer. At 1945, it removes the later feature while Saudi Arabia continues over the core. Neither seam records a regional disappearance. The two endings are software-layer changes with completely different historical meanings.

One regional card is defensible because Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, Rabigh, al-Ula, and al-Bahah sit in both decoded polygons and because Hijaz remained a meaningful place-name. The card must still label the early caliphates, Hashemite monarchy, Saudi dual kingdom, and Saudi Arabia separately every time government matters.

sections.title: Medina, Mecca, and changing political centers

items.text: The Medinan compact describes a community assembled from several groups with mutual duties and protections. It is valuable evidence for negotiated social and political membership after 622, but scholars debate its layers and setting. It should not become a modern constitution pasted over every family or settlement inside the atlas polygon.

Medina served as the first caliphs' political center after Muhammad's death in 632. Its prestige also grew through association with the Prophet, his mosque, burial, and legal traditions. Political centrality later moved elsewhere, while Medina's sacred and scholarly importance continued. Capitals can travel; holy significance is less willing to pack.

Ali transferred his caliphal seat to Kufa in 656 during the first civil war. This matters because a map labeled Hejaz across 600 to 800 can visually trap the caliphate in western Arabia. After 656, the region remained vital, but the main machinery of imperial politics was increasingly based elsewhere.

Muawiya's victory established Umayyad rule from Damascus in 661. Mecca and Medina still mattered for pilgrimage, learning, legitimacy, and opposition, yet they were not the ordinary administrative center of the empire. The early atlas layer therefore represents a region nested within larger and changing states, never an independent two-century kingdom.

Ibn al-Zubayr claimed the caliphate from Mecca during the second civil war, and his defeat in 692 restored Umayyad control. Calling this merely a smooth “Hejaz period” would erase conflict, siege, and rival sovereignty. Sacred geography could strengthen a political claim, but it did not make politics peaceful or permanent.

The Darb Zubaydah connected Kufa with Mecca across roughly 1,300 kilometers. Under Abbasid patronage, travelers found marked stations, wells, pools, dams, and settling basins. That infrastructure was an achievement in desert logistics: the road could not make the desert smaller, so engineers made water waits and journeys more survivable.

The Syrian pilgrimage road linked Damascus and Medina through a chain of stations that also preserved inscriptions. Pilgrims, officials, merchants, animals, and messages used the corridor over many centuries. A route is evidence of movement and maintenance, not a political border; travelers regularly crossed the neat colored edges that modern maps prefer.

Pilgrimage brought temporary crowds into Mecca, Medina, and Jeddah, creating work for guides, carriers, merchants, landlords, water sellers, and health officials. It also magnified shortages and disease risk. The sacred journey was therefore simultaneously religious practice, family undertaking, logistical puzzle, and a major part of the regional economy.

The Hejaz Railway reached Medina from Damascus and shortened a difficult overland journey for some pilgrims before wartime damage interrupted it. Railway stations reorganized movement and supply without replacing caravans, ships, or walking. For children watching a locomotive arrive, the loudest new animal in town ate coal and never needed dates.

Jeddah's port joined Red Sea commerce with the pilgrimage road to Mecca. Merchants and pilgrims from many regions made its streets linguistically and socially diverse. That cosmopolitan life complicates any picture of the Hijaz as culturally sealed, while surviving elite houses and official reports still reveal far more than the lives of poorer visitors.

sections.title: Homes, families, privacy, and neighborhood life

items.text: Historic Jeddah's coral-stone tower houses stacked family rooms above street-level commercial and guest spaces. Wooden screens admitted air while helping residents manage shade and privacy. A house could be home, warehouse, office, and guesthouse at once, which made “going downstairs to work” a very short commute indeed.

Roshan screens, bent entrances, reception rooms, and upper-family spaces shaped encounters between household members, guests, and the street. Architecture supported privacy without making homes socially silent. Coffeehouses, markets, mosques, and squares supplied other meeting places, so neighborhood life happened through a choreography of open, screened, public, and family spaces.

The 1916 to 1919 siege of Medina disrupted families through hunger, expulsion, separation, and military control of supplies. Oral histories preserve civilian memories that official military accounts often flatten. This is not a place for a joke: children and caregivers experienced war as missing food, absent relatives, fear, and forced movement.

Hijazi society included urban merchant households, scholarly families, artisans, pilgrimage workers, settled oasis communities, and mobile pastoral groups. Their resources and authority differed sharply. “Daily life in the Hijaz” therefore needs plural examples rather than one imaginary average family eating one standard dinner in one standard house.

Sources name rulers, diplomats, merchants, and major property owners more often than servants, laborers, women, or children. Houses and oral histories partly correct that imbalance, but neither yields a complete household census. The card treats family life as evidence from particular towns and moments, not a costume assigned to everyone for 1,345 years.

sections.title: Children, learning, and the limits of the record

items.text: Early Islamic Medina became a center for transmitting religious and legal knowledge, often through remembered reports, recitation, discussion, and writing. The sources do not provide a seventh-century class register for all Hijazi children. Learning clearly occurred, but a modern school timetable cannot be reverse-engineered from the city's later scholarly reputation.

Al-Falah School opened in Jeddah in 1905 and a related school in Mecca in 1912, offering boys free instruction that joined religious and newer subjects. It was an important institution, not proof that every boy attended or that girls received equal access. School histories are clearest about founders and curricula, quieter about truancy.

Hijazi writers argued for girls' education in the 1920s, showing that schooling women was publicly imaginable and contested before later nationwide systems. Advocacy is evidence of debate, not enrollment. No reviewed source supports claiming universal girls' schools during the atlas window, and children's home teaching remains much less visible than policy arguments.

The Islamic Institute in Mecca, founded in 1926, became an early post-primary state institution under King Abdulaziz. It trained students in religious and other subjects during the transition to Saudi rule. Its existence shows institution building after conquest, while one school still cannot represent the educational experience of every town, class, or child.

Children certainly learned language, worship, crafts, trade, animal care, and household work from relatives and specialists, but surviving sources rarely record the lesson from a child's viewpoint. The honest fun fact is a tiny one: youngsters probably asked “are we there yet?” on pilgrimage long before railways made the question arrive faster.

sections.title: Food, work, medicine, and evidence gaps

items.text: Port trade and pilgrimage sustained merchants, guides, transport workers, craftspeople, food sellers, landlords, and water suppliers. Demand rose and fell with arriving ships and caravans, so seasonal crowds shaped household income. The sources describe economic systems better than individual wages, recipes, child labor, or who washed the dishes after a crowded meal.

Jeddah repeatedly struggled to secure enough potable water for residents, soldiers, and pilgrims. Water arrived through local systems and imported supplies, and scarcity worsened when crowds grew. A cup of safe water carried engineering, labor, money, and luck; turning a tap was not yet the invisible household gesture many children know today.

Later medical writers preserve stories about physicians in the first Islamic centuries, but the narratives were copied and shaped long after the events. They can show remembered medical traditions without proving a clinic, staffing system, or treatment available to ordinary Hijazi families. The card refuses to turn famous anecdotes into a public-health network.

Archaeological access in Mecca and Medina is unusually limited, and construction has transformed ancient layers. No reviewed evidence securely reconstructs a typical seventh-century Hijazi kitchen, sickroom, schoolroom, or toilet. Absence here is a research limit, not proof that people lacked cooking, caregiving, teaching, or ways to manage waste.

International sanitary rules for pilgrimage travel addressed inspection, vaccination, quarantine, crowding, and conditions aboard pilgrim ships. Such rules reveal organized public-health ambitions in the modern period, plus anxiety about epidemics crossing ports. A regulation proves an expected standard; it does not prove every vessel was roomy, spotless, or pleasant-smelling.

sections.title: Bathrooms, sanitation, and the unglamorous infrastructure

items.text: Traditional Jeddah houses placed latrines, called taharat, in the same position on successive floors. Waste descended through a smooth plastered vertical duct to an underground stone septic tank, while a roof vent released gases. This was serious vertical engineering hidden inside houses that visitors usually remember for beautiful wooden screens.

The septic tank was generally unplastered so liquid could seep away, and accumulated material was removed about yearly. That maintenance was essential and socially invisible. Gentle truth for young readers: every splendid tower house depended on somebody handling the job least likely to appear on a souvenir postcard.

Ground-floor reception areas could be sprinkled with water for cleaning and cooling. In a hot, dusty port, that small routine joined comfort, hospitality, and hygiene. It also reminds us that sanitation included repeated household labor, not only pipes or official regulations, and that the person carrying the water deserves a place in the story.

A 1925 administrative file set sanitation requirements for ships carrying pilgrims, including inspection and public notices. Sea travel could pack strangers together for days, making ventilation, water, waste, and illness shared problems. Posted rules may have been less exciting than a ticket, but they could matter more by journey's end.

Reports from 1929 show authorities declaring the pilgrimage free of epidemic disease while nearby cholera scares still disrupted shipping. Public health depended on surveillance, trust, and international communication as well as medicine. A clean certificate was useful, but microbes remained unimpressed by official stationery and continued to require practical precautions.

sections.title: The Hashemite kingdom and its ending

items.text: Hussein ibn Ali proclaimed the Kingdom of the Hejaz in 1916 during revolt against Ottoman rule. Its authority grew from the sharifian position in Mecca, wartime alliance, and control of holy places, but international recognition and territorial claims remained complicated. The kingdom was a specific modern monarchy, not the early-Islamic region revived unchanged.

Medina remained under Ottoman command through a long siege ending in 1919, even after the wider war had turned. Civilian suffering, expulsions, and contested memories complicate triumphant revolt stories. A kingdom proclaimed in Mecca did not instantly possess every city that later maps color the same shade.

Saudi forces captured Taif and Mecca in 1924, while Hussein abdicated and his son Ali continued resistance. Medina and Jeddah surrendered in 1925. The sequence matters: “conquest of Hejaz” was not one instantaneous recoloring, and the atlas's unchanged 1920-to-1930 polygon hides the political break inside a single shape.

Ali's surrender at Jeddah in December 1925 ended the Hashemite Kingdom of the Hejaz. People, pilgrimage, houses, schools, and regional identity continued under a new ruler. Political ending and social continuity can both be true, which is why this card does not use either 1945 or timeless regional survival as the monarchy's end date.

South Asian Muslims and other outside observers debated how the holy places should be governed during 1919 to 1926. Their proposals reveal the Hijaz's international religious importance and local diversity. They also show that residents were discussed by distant publics, sometimes as symbols, while living through taxes, shortages, war, and institutional change.

sections.title: Saudi rule, renaming, and the false 1945 ending

items.text: Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz in 1926 after conquest. The title marked a real transfer of sovereignty, yet governing a recently conquered, pilgrimage-centered region required accommodation as well as command. The atlas cannot show that transition because its 1920 and 1930 features use exactly the same geometry and id.

The 1927 Treaty of Jeddah recognized the complete independence of Ibn Saud's dominions and used the title King of the Hejaz and Nejd and Dependencies. This was a dual kingdom under one ruler, not the surviving Hashemite state. Treaty wording supplies secure contemporary evidence for the political name after conquest.

A royal order in 1932 renamed the combined realm the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. From then on, “Hejaz” named a region within the Saudi state rather than an internationally separate kingdom. The atlas nevertheless overlays hejaz-1920 and Saudi Arabia together in 1938, an internal clue that its layers mix region and state.

Saudi Arabia entered the United Nations in 1945. That event belongs to the continuing Saudi state, not to a Kingdom of Hejaz that ended twenty years earlier. The atlas removes its Hejaz overlay at 1945 because of dataset design; no reviewed source identifies a matching conquest, abolition, or depopulation.

At the 1938-to-1945 seam, Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, Rabigh, al-Ula, and al-Bahah simply lose the Hejaz overlay and remain inside Saudi Arabia. Sana'a changes to a Yemen layer, exposing the modern polygon's overreach. This is a cartographic cleanup, not a single historical event across all those places.

sections.title: Arabic voices on rock, stamp, and royal order

items.text: Early written-language sample: “أنا زهير كتبت زمن توفي عمر سنة أربع وعشرين”. Transliteration: “anā Zuhayr, katabtu zamana tuwuffiya ʿUmar, sanat arbaʿ wa-ʿishrīn.” Translation: “I, Zuhayr, wrote this when Umar died, in the year twenty-four.” The rock graffito dates securely to 24 AH, 644 to 645 CE.

The Zuhayr inscription stands at Qa al-Mutadil on the route between al-Ula and Hegra. Its short first-person sentence gives a named writer and a datable response to Caliph Umar's death. It is not a diary of all Hijazi life, but a rare voice that reached us without a court historian speaking over it.

Modern written-language sample from a 1922 Hejaz stamp: “الحكومة العربية الهاشمية”. Transliteration: “al-Ḥukūmah al-ʿArabiyyah al-Hāshimiyyah.” Translation: “The Hashemite Arab Government.” The small official inscription securely belongs to the Hashemite era and must not be presented as Saudi wording or as evidence for seventh-century government.

A stamp moved government language through ordinary hands: postal clerks, merchants, travelers, and families sending news. Its inscription asserted Hashemite authority while its journey depended on practical networks. The stamp is tiny enough to lose in a pocket, yet politically loud enough to announce who claimed to run the post office.

Later official Arabic named the state “المملكة العربية السعودية”, transliterated “al-Mamlakah al-ʿArabiyyah al-Suʿūdiyyah,” the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The 1932 name marks a new state framework after conquest and dual monarchy. Putting it beside the 1922 stamp lets children see political change in actual words rather than one unchanging map label.

ending.text: This shared card contains two political endings and two cartographic seams. The early “hejaz” layer disappears at 800 when the atlas assigns the region to an Abbasid feature. The Hijaz itself did not vanish, and Abbasid authority had already begun in 750. The Hashemite Kingdom of the Hejaz ended much later, after Saudi forces captured its cities and Ali surrendered Jeddah in December 1925. Ibn Saud then ruled the Kingdom of the Hejaz and Nejd; the 1927 Treaty of Jeddah recognized that dual kingdom, and a 1932 order renamed the combined state the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The atlas still carries “hejaz-1920” through its 1938 snapshot, layered with Saudi Arabia, and removes it only at 1945. That endpoint records no matching fall. Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Taif, Yanbu, Rabigh, al-Ula, and al-Bahah remain under Saudi coverage, while regional Hijazi identity, pilgrimage, families, institutions, and buildings continue. The card therefore marks regional continuity, keeps fell null for both atlas records, and names no 1945 successor. The Hashemite monarchy's real political ending stays in 1925, where history puts it.
